stories.headline: Torrential rains trigger flash floods in Kashmir parts, heavy rains lash Jammu
stories.title: Torrential rains trigger flash floods in Kashmir parts, heavy rains lash Jammu
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 19: Torrential rains triggered flash floods in parts of Kashmir on Wednesday, while heavy showers lashed Jammu, swelling rivers and streams as the Meteorological Centre Srinagar ruled out widespread rainfall but warned of more intense localised weather. In Shopian, showers in Shadab Kareva swelled a local stream. Water, mud and slush flowed through the area. Flash floods were also reported in Dachnoo and Herpora. Overflowing streams entered orchards. A flash flood also hit Baderhma village. Flash floods were reported from Haknar and Gund in Ganderbal. Upper Batkoot in Pahalgam, Anantnag, also witnessed flooding. Road connectivity and water supply were affected. Batkoot has witnessed at least five such incidents during intense showers and cloudbursts. Gusty winds also disrupted normal life in parts of Kashmir. Jammu recorded 88.7 mm of rain. Banihal received 20.7 mm, Batote 28.8 mm, Katra 48.2 mm, Bhaderwah 1.8 mm, Kathua 76.6 mm, Jammu Airport 33 mm, Udhampur 32.2 mm, Ramban 6.5 mm, Samba 85 mm, Poonch 1.5 mm, Reasi 39 mm and Doda 9 mm. Rajouri and Kishtwar recorded traces. The rains swelled rivers and streams across parts of Jammu. Kathua faced the highest risk of a rapid rise in water levels, followed by Samba. Authorities issued a red alert. People were advised to stay away from water bodies and low-lying areas. Temperatures in Jammu remained below normal. Kashmir stayed near normal. Jammu recorded 27.4 degrees Celsius, 5.7 degrees below normal. Banihal recorded 23.2 degrees Celsius, Batote 23.7 degrees Celsius, Katra 24.6 degrees Celsius, and Bhaderwah 25 degrees Celsius. Srinagar recorded 31.6 degrees Celsius, Qazigund recorded 28 degrees Celsius, Pahalgam 25.2 degrees Celsius, Kupwara 32.5 degrees Celsius, Kokernag 26.5 degrees Celsius, and Gulmarg 20.4 degrees Celsius. Temperatures remained close to normal. The MeT forecast generally hot and humid conditions from August 19 to 22. Light to moderate rain and thundershowers are likely at scattered to many places. Brief intense showers may occur in a few districts during the early morning and afternoon. From August 23 to 27, brief rain and thundershowers are likely at scattered places. These are expected mainly during the early morning and afternoon. The department warned that intense localised showers could trigger flash floods, mudslides, and landslides. People were advised to avoid rivers, streams, nallahs, and landslide-prone areas. They were also asked to follow local advisories. Farmers may continue harvesting and other farm operations. The latest weather events come amid a series of monsoon-related disasters in J&K in which more than 30 people have died. Roads, homes, farmland, and livestock have also been damaged. Flash floods and landslides in Poonch and Rajouri on July 19 killed more than 25 people. Earlier cloudbursts caused widespread damage in Doda, Kishtwar and Ramban. Director MeT Srinagar Mukhtar Ahmad said rainfall would remain largely localised. Parts of Jammu division could, however, receive intense showers. “The intense, brief thundershowers and cloudbursts are a recurring phenomenon during the monsoon,” Ahmad said. IRFAN RAINA REPORTS FROM KANGAN Two low-intensity flash floods struck Haknar and Wangath areas in Kangan sub division of Ganderbal district on Wednesday following a brief spell of intense rainfall. Despite initial panic among locals, official reports confirmed that the twin surges caused no casualties, no injuries, and no structural damage to property. The incidents occurred in quick succession along two local streams (nallahs) in the upper reaches of the Kangan sub-division. Sudden torrential downpours upstream led to a rapid rise in water levels, carrying silt, loose rocks, and mud down toward the main road stretches. Local authorities, along with teams from the J&K Police, State Disaster Response Force (SDRF), rushed to the spot. "The situation was brought under control quickly as water levels receded,” said an official. "There has been no damage to residential homes, commercial property, or livestock." M M PARVAIZ REPORTS FROM RAMBAN Despite intermittent rainfall, fresh mudslides, and waterlogging at several vulnerable locations, the Srinagar-Jammu National Highway remained open for regulated two-way traffic on Wednesday. However, movement of traffic remained slow at several stretches, officials said. Traffic authorities said that the Udhampur-Chenani section of the highway, which has remained vulnerable to landslides during the ongoing spell of rain, remained open. Rain-induced waterlogging and mudslides at Dewal and other locations affected the smooth flow of traffic. Traffic movement remained particularly slow at Dewal in Udhampur district, where vehicles were being regulated through an approximately 40-metre damaged, uneven and undulating single-lane stretch. Ongoing road improvement and highway construction works further contributed to intermittent congestion. Similar conditions prevailed on the Maroog-Kishtwari Pather stretch in Ramban district, where traffic was being regulated through a single-lane portion amid ongoing construction activity and damaged road conditions. The movement of heavy vehicles was particularly slow at the vulnerable locations. Earlier in the day, traffic on the highway was disrupted for some time after a mudslide blocked the road near a construction site at Nagrota in Jammu, leaving vehicles stranded in long queues. NHAI men and machinery were immediately pressed into service, and the debris and muck were subsequently cleared with the help of dumpers, restoring vehicular movement. Later, following heavy rains a huge mudslide hit and blocked the road in Khari Tharad area of Udhampur, however, it was cleared for traffic. Traffic congestion persisted for some time after the road was reopened due to slippery road conditions and the accumulation of vehicles during the disruption. Meanwhile, restoration work on the Srinagar-bound road tube at Dhramthal near Samroli in Udhampur district continued despite persistent rainfall. An NHAI official said men and machinery remained deployed at the site, but rain was hampering the restoration operation. The Srinagar-bound tube was blocked on Sunday evening after a massive landslide brought a large quantity of debris onto the carriageway. Following the incident, traffic was diverted from Samroli through the alternate Jammu-bound road tube. Officials said the massive debris slide is likely to take a couple of days to clear completely. To facilitate traffic movement in the meantime, inter-lane ramps have been carved out at both ends of the affected stretch to bypass the slide zone. They said the restoration of the affected tube is expected to take at least four to five days. The NHAI has also been asked to widen and smoothen the inter-lane ramps to facilitate the movement of commuters, particularly large trailers and bulk carriers, through the restricted section. The temporary arrangement has allowed up- and down-bound traffic to continue moving through the respective tubes. However, traffic authorities said the arrangement requires careful regulation because of the restricted road width. The down tube in the vicinity has also been reduced to a single lane at two to three locations following erosion triggered by recent rains. SSP Traffic National Highway Raja Adil Hameed said the highway remained open for two-way traffic, while traffic personnel were regulating movement at vulnerable stretches. Traffic authorities said that, subject to fair weather and satisfactory road conditions, the highway is expected to remain open for regulated two-way traffic on Thursday. Passenger vehicles, private cars, and goods carriers will be permitted to ply in both directions, subject to the condition of the highway and clearance of any fresh obstructions. Authorities have advised commuters to check the latest highway status before commencing their journey and remain in contact with the Traffic Control Units at Jammu, Ramban and Srinagar. Passengers and Light Motor Vehicle (LMV) operators have been particularly advised to undertake travel between Ramban and Banihal during daylight hours and avoid unnecessary night journeys due to the risk of shooting stones, landslides, and other weather-related hazards. Motorists have been urged to maintain lane discipline, avoid overtaking and wrong-lane driving, and refrain from unnecessary stoppages at vulnerable locations to prevent further congestion. Truck operators carrying fresh and perishable commodities and livestock have been directed to adhere strictly to prescribed loading norms. Heavy vehicle operators have also been advised to avoid overloading, ensure proper vehicle fitness and carry adequate fuel in view of possible delays. Officials cautioned that the highway status could change at short notice in the event of fresh landslides, mudslides, or deterioration in weather and road conditions, and urged travellers to follow official traffic advisories before and during their journey.

stories.headline: Beyond Military Zones : Kashmir’s LoC areas emerge as new tourism hotspots
stories.title: Beyond Military Zones : Kashmir’s LoC areas emerge as new tourism hotspots
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 19: For decades, areas along the Line of Control (LoC) in Kashmir were known mainly for security installations, checkpoints and military activity. Today, several of these remote areas are slowly gaining attention as emerging tourist destinations. Places such as Keran, Tangdhar, Uri and Gurez are seeing growing interest as improved infrastructure and a sustained ceasefire have made travel easier. The change is giving visitors a chance to explore areas that remained largely outside the traditional tourism circuit. Tangdhar Valley, reached through the Sadhna Pass, offers mountain views, alpine meadows and access to remote villages. Travellers, however, need to plan carefully around security checks and changing weather conditions. Teetwal, located along the Kishanganga River, is also attracting visitors interested in Kashmir’s history and culture. The restored Sharada Temple has added to the area’s appeal among pilgrims, researchers and heritage enthusiasts. Uri offers another perspective on the region’s history. The Aman Setu, associated with cross-LoC links, remains an important landmark reflecting the area’s strategic and political past. Further north, Gurez Valley offers visitors an opportunity to experience the culture of the Dard-Shin community. Traditional wooden houses, mountain landscapes and the prominent Habba Khatoon Peak remain among its major attractions. The growing interest in these areas is different from conventional mass tourism. Visitors are increasingly looking for history, culture, local experiences and lesser-known landscapes. The trend could also support local communities through homestays, transport services, guides, handicrafts and small businesses. At the same time, tourism authorities and local residents face the challenge of protecting the fragile Himalayan environment. As more frontier villages enter Kashmir’s tourism map, the focus is shifting from security-only narratives to community-led tourism, cultural preservation and sustainable economic opportunities.

stories.headline: J&K an important part of India: US envoy
stories.title: J&K an important part of India: US envoy
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 19: United States Ambassador Sergio Gor on Wednesday described Jammu and Kashmir as “an important part of India” during his first visit to the Union Territory. Gor, who also serves as President Donald Trump’s Special Envoy for South and Central Asia, made the remarks after a meeting with Chief Minister Omar Abdullah at the latter’s Gupkar residence. Standing alongside Abdullah, he told reporters: “As everybody here knows, I am the US ambassador to India. And this is an important part of India. And so I’m here visiting for the first time. It is an incredibly beautiful place and I am thrilled to be here.” The two-day visit to J&K and Ladakh is the first standalone trip by a serving US ambassador to J&K and Ladakh since the abrogation of Article 370 in 2019 and the reorganisation of the erstwhile state into two Union Territories. It is also the first such engagement after the April 2025 Pahalgam terror attack, in which 26 tourists were killed, and India’s subsequent Operation Sindoor. The last meeting between a serving US ambassador and a sitting J&K CM took place in 2011, when Timothy Roemer called on Omar Abdullah. The last standalone visit by a US envoy was by Kenneth Juster in 2018. Gor described the interaction as “very warm” and “very cordial.” In a post on X, he said he had appreciated the chance to learn about CM Omar’s priorities. “We discussed ways to deepen economic collaboration and create opportunities that would mutually benefit both of our nations,” he said. One of the most closely watched remarks concerned the US travel advisory. The State Department currently maintains a Level 4 “do not travel” warning for J&K (except eastern Ladakh and Leh), citing terrorism and civil unrest. The advisory has long been a concern for the J&K administration as it seeks to attract more international tourists. Gor indicated Washington would examine whether it should be downgraded. “The United States puts out travel warnings. And every so often we re-evaluate travel warnings. I cannot make any big announcements here today, but it is something we are going to look at,” he said. Gor credited New Delhi, CM Omar, and the J&K government with having “made some incredible steps toward keeping this area safer and making it more secure.” “So we will be looking at whether the travel warning that is recommended by the United States is something that should be downgraded. This is a beautiful area. I think a lot of Americans would enjoy coming here and seeing the beauty and the opportunities that exist here,” he said. No formal change was announced. Officials said that any revision would follow a standard review process in Washington. A team of US diplomats from the embassy in New Delhi had called on National Conference President Farooq Abdullah a day earlier as part of preparations for the visit. Kashmir’s chief cleric, Mirwaiz Umar Farooq, welcomed the ambassador’s arrival and expressed hope that he would engage with a broad cross-section of people. PDP President Mehbooba Mufti urged Gor to review and withdraw the travel advisory, describing it as a barrier for families dependent on tourism. Gor’s comments, particularly the explicit description of J&K as an important part of India, are being viewed in New Delhi and Srinagar as a notable diplomatic signal amid Pakistan’s continued claims on the region. The visit comes as India-US strategic ties have deepened, including in defence and intelligence sharing following earlier tensions along the Line of Actual Control. The ambassador’s Ladakh leg on Thursday will mark another first: the first visit there by a US ambassador since the 2020 Galwan clashes.

stories.headline: Christianity & Kashmir: A Shared Legacy
stories.title: Christianity & Kashmir: A Shared Legacy
stories.summary: Christianity and Kashmir have a shared legacy as Christian missionaries have played a pivotal role in laying the foundation of education system in this beautiful land that left a lasting imprint on its social and intellectual development. Roots of the Christian educators can be traced back to late 19th century when they introduced the concept of structured schooling, modern subjects, physical training and girls’ education in the Valley.Classrooms of the missionary schools brought together children from different communities. These institutions became spaces where education, friendship, sport, discipline and shared experiences often transcended religious boundaries. Long before phrases such as interfaith dialogue and social cohesion became part of public vocabulary, generations of Kashmiris experienced diversity naturally inside these institutions. Across Kashmir, former students of Christian missionary schools became doctors, engineers,administrators, politicians, religious leaders, diplomats, academics, entrepreneurs, journalists,lawyers, artists, industrialists, hoteliers and public servants. Some remained in Kashmir. Others carried their education across India and around the world. Stories of these students form an important part of Kashmir’s modern social history and drive home a point that a school can have a religious identity and still make an educational contribution to a society much larger than that religious community. TYNDALE BISCOE SCHOOL A significant milestone in the educational history of Kashmir came in 1880, when the Church Mission Society established a school in Srinagar under Reverend J. Hinton Knowles. The institution gradually developed into the educational tradition associated with Tyndale Biscoe. Canon Cecil Tyndale-Biscoe, who joined the school in the 1890s, left a lasting imprint through his emphasis on discipline, physical education, self-reliance, service and character. Its alumni reflect the remarkable diversity. They include Dr Farooq Abdullah, former Chief Minister of Jammu and Kashmir; Aga Syed Ruhullah Mehdi, Member of Parliament from Srinagar; Moulvi Imran Raza Ansari, prominent Shia cleric and political leader; Dr Anil Bhan, renowned cardiac surgeon and P. N. Dhar, economist and former senior adviser to Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. The institution’s alumni also include first IAS topper from J&K, Shah Faesal. MALLINSON GIRLS’ SCHOOL Mallinson Girls’ School was established in October 1912 by Miss Violet B. Fitze as the Girls’ Mission High School, initially operating from a modest mud house at Fateh Kadal in Srinagar’s old city. Fitze, a missionary educator, founded the institution under the auspices of the Church Missionary Society (CMS), marking it as a dedicated effort to introduce formal schooling for girls in the region. In the mid-20th century, the CMS Girls School at Fateh Kadal in Srinagar, faced increasing enrolment and spatial constraints due to its rapid growth under missionary leadership. By the late 1950s, the decision was made to relocate the institution to a more expansive site near Lal Chowk area. The move was completed in 1962, coinciding with the retirement of principal Miss Muriel P. Mallinson after her 40-year tenure from 1922 to 1962, and positioned the school adjacent to the CMS Boys’ School (now Tyndale Biscoe School), facilitating shared infrastructure on a donated plot that supported further development. ST JOSEPH’S SCHOOL BARAMULLA Another important institution St Joseph’s Higher Secondary School Baramulla in North Kashmir was established by the Mill Hill Fathers or Mill Hill Missionaries from London in 1903 for everyone without any distinction of religion, caste, creed or colour. It was run by Society of Jesus after Mill Hill Missionaries left the mission. Among its distinguished alumni was Dr Mohammad Najibullah, who later became President of Afghanistan. His journey from a school in Baramulla to the presidency of Afghanistan is a remarkable example of how far the influence of a Kashmiri educational institution could travel. The school’s alumni also include figures former minister and a senior politician Syed Altaf Bukhari, former bureaucrat Muhammad Ashraf Bukhari and others. PRESENTATION CONVENT The Presentation Convent was founded in 1936 by Sisters Peter Conway, Sacred Heart, Annunciata, and Xavier—who relocated from Rawalpindi at the invitation of Maharaja Hari Singh—the school commenced operations in Srinagar before shifting to its current 10-acre site at Rajbagh in Srinagar along the Jhelum River in 1939, with initial government support for land lease and construction. The school was initially started as the Senior Cambridge School. The school closed down temporarily following the Pakistani invasion that occurred during the India-Pakistan War of 1947–1948. The school was restarted by Fr. J. Boerkamp in 1956 as the founding father and the first principal of the school he rendered yeomen service to the cause of education in the valley. His journey from a Srinagar school to one of the country’s highest diplomatic positions is a remarkable example of the reach of education. The alumni story also includes Haseeb Drabu, economist, former Finance Minister of Jammu and Kashmir and former Chairman of Jammu & Kashmir Bank; Agha Shahid Ali, the internationally acclaimed poet; Rohit Bal, one of India’s best-known fashion designers. It gave me an opportunity to engage directly with young people, understand their aspirations and concerns, and appreciate the importance of giving a voice to those who often feel unheard. Looking back, I see that experience as part of the wider confidence, discipline and sense of civic responsibility that education helped cultivate in me. And among the political alumni are the Lone brothers, whose association with Burn Hall adds yet another dimension to the institution’s long and diverse public legacy. My wife is a practising Christian from South India who has made Kashmir her home and has worked in a senior administrative and human resources role at a missionary school in Srinagar. Both my daughters have also received their high-school education at Presentation Convent School in Srinagar. For our family, therefore, Christian education in Kashmir is not simply a subject of history. It is part of our lived experience. I experienced it as a student. My wife has experienced it as a Christian professional working within the educational tradition. My daughters have experienced it as students. Our association with interfaith engagement has also extended beyond Kashmir. My wife and I have been associated with US-based interfaith organisations and initiatives that promote dialogue, understanding and cooperation among people of different faiths. Those experiences have reinforced a simple belief: interfaith harmony does not require us to erase our differences. It requires us to respect those differences while finding common ground. In our own home, this understanding is lived rather than merely discussed. We celebrate Eid and Christmas together, sharing in each other’s traditions with respect and affection. For us, this does not diminish either faith. It reflects something more fundamental — family, love, friendship and mutual respect. He is a regular columnist for Greater Kashmir, has worked with national and international news organizations, and has authored books on Kashmir.

Some remained in Kashmir.
Others carried their education across India and around the world.

stories.headline: Getting it right, not getting it wrong
stories.title: Getting it right, not getting it wrong
stories.summary: When a contractor’s Input Tax Credit worth over ten crores goes silent overnight, the taxpayer feels the shock first. But behind every Rule 86A action lies a department that has, at some point, formed a considered view that revenue is at risk — from fake invoicing, circular trading, or credit claimed without any underlying supply. The Hon’ble High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh at Srinagar, vide judgment dated 12.08.2026 in NCC Limited [WP(C) 1935/2026], set aside the departmental communication blocking Input Tax Credit (ITC) of ₹10,45,38,432/-. Read quickly, this can look like a setback for the department. Read properly, it is nothing of the kind — it is the Court doing exactly what judiciary should do: telling the department how to make its orders and actions bullet proof, rather than telling it to stop enforcing. The power itself was never in doubt The most important line in the entire order is easy to miss because it comes almost as an afterthought: the Bench expressly clarified that setting aside the communication “shall not come in the way of the Competent Authority... to pass an appropriate order under Rule 86-A... after providing the petitioner an adequate opportunity of being heard.” Read that again. The Court did not say the department was wrong to suspect the credit. It did not say Rs. 10.45 crore was safe. It did not restore the credit to NCC Limited’s ledger without conditions. It simply sent the case back with an instruction: do it again, and do it with reasons on record and a hearing given. That is not a defeat for the department — it is a second chance to issue an order that will actually survive scrutiny at every subsequent stage, from appeal to Tribunal to writ court. This matters because an order that is set aside on a technical or procedural ground is an order the department gets to correct. An order that survives on a weak procedural foundation but is later challenged on merits, after years of litigation, is a far costlier outcome for revenue. The NCC Limited Judgement should be read by every GST Officer as a warning against the wrong kind of risk — not the risk of blocking bogus credit, but the risk of handing the taxpayer an easy exit route on a paperwork lapse. A useful discipline, not a new burden Rule 86A already required “reasons to believe,” recorded in writing, before any blocking order could be passed. That requirement was never optional; it was built into the rule from the outset precisely so that the power would be used with rigour and not casually. What the J&K High Court has done — following the Karnataka High Court in K-9 Enterprises (whose SLP the Supreme Court dismissed) and the Telangana High Court in Bhavani Oxides — is read a further, closely related discipline into the same provision: a short opportunity of hearing before the block, given how adversely it affects the taxpayer’s cash flow and business operations. Far from weakening the department’s hand, this discipline strengthens it. A blocking order preceded by even a brief notice, and grounded in specific, recorded reasons — mismatches in GSTR-2B, absence of proof of actual receipt of goods, non-existent or non-functional suppliers, values inconsistent with e-way bill trails — becomes far harder for any taxpayer’s counsel to dislodge on appeal. It converts a suspicion into a documented finding. Officers who already build their Rule 86A cases this way — recording the specific red flags, will find that this judgment changes nothing about how they already work. It simply makes explicit the standard the best GST cases were always meeting. What this means going forward For GST Officers, the message from NCC Limited Judgement is not caution but confidence: use Rule 86A firmly against every genuine case of fraudulent or ineligible credit, but build the case the way the law always intended — reasons recorded before the order is signed, a short notice or hearing given wherever the urgency of the situation allows it, and the blocked quantum tied transparently to the credit balance actually standing in the ledger. Orders built this way do not get set aside; they get upheld, and they send the clearest possible signal to habitual evaders that the department’s enforcement machinery is both vigorous and legally unassailable. The department’s interest is never served by a shortcut. It is served by a Rule 86A order that a taxpayer’s lawyer reads and decides not to challenge at all. (The author is a State Taxes Officer posted at Circle-C, Srinagar. Views are personal.)

stories.headline: PDP protests at Jablipora Fruit Mandi, seeks crop insurance
stories.title: PDP protests at Jablipora Fruit Mandi, seeks crop insurance
stories.summary: Anantnag, Aug 19: PDP leader Iltija Mufti on Wednesday led a protest at the Jablipora Fruit Mandi, demanding that the Jammu and Kashmir government introduce a comprehensive crop insurance scheme for apple growers, waive Kisan Credit Card (KCC) loans and establish a green corridor for the smooth transport of fruit to markets outside the Union Territory. Speaking during the protest, Mufti said apple farmers in Jammu and Kashmir suffer “huge losses every year due to highway closures” and are neither provided crop insurance nor given relief on the large KCC loans they have taken to sustain their orchards. She said farmers receive “no compensation” whenever weather calamities, including floods, flash floods and hailstorms, strike the region. “I am merely asking that they be given subsidies and that a crop insurance scheme be introduced,” she said. “We know that horticulture in Jammu and Kashmir is a legitimate means of livelihood, through which people support their families. The entire economy of Jammu and Kashmir has been run by people associated with horticulture,” she added, describing horticulture as the backbone of the region’s economy. Mufti said the fruit mandi was the epicentre of trade for the region’s produce and referred to an earlier attempt by PDP workers and leaders from Shopian, including Aijaz Ahmad and Raja Waheed, to protest at the Shopian fruit mandi. She said they were placed under house arrest by police. She said raising issues concerning students and farmers was part of her political responsibility and objected to attempts to give the issue a political colour. “There is nothing personal for me in this, but the condition of Jammu and Kashmir’s farmers is extremely bad,” she said. Mufti criticised the elected government’s handling of the issue, saying that despite receiving a large mandate, it had failed to act on demands concerning farmers. She questioned the delay in decisions on a KCC loan waiver, subsidies and a crop insurance scheme, which she said fall within the Chief Minister’s domain. Referring to Chief Minister Omar Abdullah’s remarks ahead of his meeting with US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor, Mufti questioned his approach and called on him to show greater resolve. Abdullah had said he would discuss Jammu and Kashmir and the situation in the region with Gor but would not take complaints about internal issues to the US envoy or seek their resolution from Washington. “We expect better from the Chief Minister of Jammu and Kashmir. We expect him to step up. We expect him to fight for the rights and dignity of our people, whether it is farmers, open merit students or Gen Z,” she said, alleging that the Chief Minister appeared to be under pressure. In a post on X following the protest, Mufti said the demands included a comprehensive insurance scheme for apple farmers, a waiver of KCC loans and a green corridor, adding that “Kashmir’s horticulture cannot be left in the lurch.”
